The Python internship in short

In the SkillMe Python internship you build one of 3 projects, such as PyAnalytics: Local Automation & Data Processing Hub, a project where you build a friendly Python tool that reads your spending data from CSV files, cleans it up and turns it into clear reports, ending with a small web dashboard. In week 1 you write a small Python program that reads a CSV file of expenses and prints useful totals in the terminal. By week 4 you put a small web dashboard on top of your database using Flask, and protect your core logic with a few automated tests. Each milestone is posted on LinkedIn and checked against that week's checklist before it counts. Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month.

Week by week

What each week of the Python internship covers

Shown for PyAnalytics: Local Automation & Data Processing Hub. The other projects follow the same four-week shape.

  1. Week 1 of 4

    Read a CSV and Summarise It

    Beginner2-3 hours

    Write a small Python program that reads a CSV file of expenses and prints useful totals in the terminal. This is the foundation of the whole project, and it practises the everyday Python skills (functions, loops, files and dictionaries) that every later week depends on.

    What you learn

    • Reading files safely with with open(...) and the built-in csv module
    • Splitting a program into small functions that each do one job
    • Using dictionaries to group and total values by category
    • Building a simple text menu with input() and a while loop

    What you submit

    • main.py with separate functions for loading, totalling and displaying data
    • A sample data/expenses.csv file with at least 15 rows
    • A working menu-driven CLI you can run with python main.py
    • A README with run instructions and a screenshot of the output
    How week 1 is reviewed
    • Running python main.py shows a menu and each option prints the correct result
    • The category totals add up to the overall total printed by the program
    • Choosing Quit exits cleanly without an error
    • The code has at least four functions and no copy-pasted logic

    Stretch goal: Add a menu option that shows totals per month by taking the first 7 characters of the date (for example 2025-03).

  2. Week 2 of 4

    Classes, Modules and Clean Data

    Beginner+2-3 hours

    Reorganise your code into classes and modules, and make it handle messy real-world data. You will also let users add new expenses and export a report, so the tool starts to feel like a real app.

    What you learn

    • Writing classes with __init__ and methods (an Expense and an ExpenseTracker)
    • Splitting code into modules and importing between files
    • Cleaning and validating data such as blank rows, bad numbers and extra spaces
    • Writing data back to files as CSV and JSON

    What you submit

    • tracker.py, storage.py and main.py modules with classes in use
    • A loader that reports how many bad rows it skipped
    • New menu options for adding, searching and exporting
    • A generated report.json committed as a sample output
    How week 2 is reviewed
    • The program runs without crashing on a CSV that contains blank and invalid rows
    • A newly added expense still appears after you quit and restart the program
    • Searching for a word finds matches regardless of capital letters
    • report.json opens and contains the correct category totals
    • main.py contains only menu code and the logic lives in the classes

    Stretch goal: Let the user set a monthly budget per category and show a warning next to any category that goes over it.

  3. Week 3 of 4

    Save to SQLite and Handle Errors

    Intermediate2-3 hours

    Replace the CSV file with a real SQLite database using Python's built-in sqlite3 module, and add proper command-line arguments. This teaches you how most apps store data and how to make a program fail gracefully.

    What you learn

    • Creating tables and running INSERT and SELECT queries with sqlite3
    • Using parameterised queries (? placeholders) to avoid SQL injection
    • Handling errors with try/except and giving clear messages
    • Adding command-line arguments and subcommands with argparse

    What you submit

    • db.py with table creation and query functions
    • CLI subcommands import, add and summary (with --month)
    • Friendly error messages for missing files and bad input
    • An updated README listing every command with an example
    How week 3 is reviewed
    • Running import twice on the same file does not crash and either skips duplicates or shows a clear message
    • summary prints the same totals as your Week 2 version for the same data
    • Passing a file that does not exist prints a clear error, not a Python traceback
    • All SQL uses ? placeholders instead of f-strings
    • python main.py --help lists all the commands

    Stretch goal: Add a delete <id> command and an export --format csv command that writes the database back out to a CSV file.

  4. Week 4 of 4

    Web Dashboard, Tests and Demo

    Intermediate+2-3 hours

    Put a small web dashboard on top of your database using Flask, and protect your core logic with a few automated tests. You finish with a complete, documented project that you can demo in under a minute.

    What you learn

    • Creating routes and HTML templates with Flask
    • Handling a simple HTML form with GET and POST
    • Writing unit tests with pytest
    • Writing a clear README for someone who has never seen your project

    What you submit

    • A Flask dashboard with summary, expense list and add-expense pages
    • At least 4 passing pytest tests
    • requirements.txt and a complete README with screenshots
    • A 30-60 second demo video
    How week 4 is reviewed
    • flask --app app run opens a dashboard at http://127.0.0.1:5000
    • Adding an expense through the form shows it on the list page straight away
    • Submitting the form with an invalid amount shows an error instead of saving
    • pytest runs at least 4 tests and all of them pass
    • A new person can set up and run the project by following only the README

    Stretch goal: Add a bar chart of category totals using Chart.js from a CDN, or a button that downloads the monthly report as a CSV file.

Python internship: questions and answers

What will I build in the Python internship?

You are assigned one of 3 projects: PyAnalytics: Local Automation & Data Processing Hub, PySentinel: Automated Web Intelligence & System Monitor or QuizCraft: Flashcard & Quiz Trainer. Each is a single project built up over four weekly milestones, so each week adds to the last.

What skills will I learn in the Python internship?

The Python internship works with Python 3, OOP and APIs. Week 1: reading files safely with with open(...) and the built-in csv module; splitting a program into small functions that each do one job. Week 2: writing classes with __init__ and methods (an Expense and an ExpenseTracker); splitting code into modules and importing between files. Week 3: creating tables and running INSERT and SELECT queries with sqlite3; using parameterised queries (? placeholders) to avoid SQL injection. Week 4: creating routes and HTML templates with Flask; handling a simple HTML form with GET and POST.

Do I need experience to apply for the Python internship?

You need the basics of Python 3, OOP and APIs, not prior internship experience. Week 1 starts at beginner level, where you write a small Python program that reads a CSV file of expenses and prints useful totals in the terminal. Week 4 reaches intermediate+ level. A short screening quiz (8 questions, about 5 minutes) checks you are ready to start.

How is each Python milestone reviewed?

Every week has a checklist, and a milestone is approved only when it meets all of it. For week 1 of PyAnalytics: Local Automation & Data Processing Hub, that means: running python main.py shows a menu and each option prints the correct result; the category totals add up to the overall total printed by the program; choosing Quit exits cleanly without an error; the code has at least four functions and no copy-pasted logic. Reviewers include engineers who work at Walmart, Google and LinkedIn, and work that misses the bar comes back with notes.

What can I put on my resume after the Python internship?

Each approved milestone gives you a line you can back up with a public LinkedIn post: Built a menu-driven Python CLI that reads expense data from a CSV file; Wrote reusable functions to calculate totals, category breakdowns and the biggest expense; Formatted clean terminal reports using f-strings and dictionaries; Refactored my Python expense tool into classes and separate modules; Added data cleaning that safely skips invalid rows instead of crashing; Built add, search and JSON export features into the command-line app; Moved my Python expense tracker from CSV files to a SQLite database; Built a command-line interface with argparse subcommands and filters; Added error handling so the tool shows clear messages instead of crashing; Built a Flask web dashboard on top of my SQLite expense tracker; Wrote automated pytest tests for my data cleaning and reporting logic; Shipped a complete, documented Python project with both a CLI and a web interface.

What are the other projects in the Python internship?

PySentinel: Automated Web Intelligence & System Monitor: Build a Python monitor that checks your computer's health and whether your favourite websites are up, and tells you when something goes wrong. QuizCraft: Flashcard & Quiz Trainer: Build a quiz and flashcard app that helps you revise any subject, starting in the terminal and ending as a small web app. Every project follows the same four-week shape, with one reviewed milestone a week.

Is the Python internship paid? Is there a stipend?

Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month. It is performance-based and goes to the interns whose reviewed Python work stands out in their cohort, not to every intern.

How much time does it take?

4 weeks, one milestone a week, each planned for about 2-3 hours. It is fully remote and open worldwide, so you work around college or a job.
